query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially reducing the Mo content by substituting part of it with additional Nb will decrease the overall electronegativity difference in the alloy, which in turn will improve room‐temperature ductility while largely preserving the solid solution strengthening that underpins high yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC solid solution with a compressive yield strength of about 1719 MPa but limited plasticity at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Replace a portion of Mo with Nb (e.g., a ~25% reduction in Mo with a corresponding increase in Nb) to adjust the alloy’s composition while retaining the disordered BCC phase.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compression tests performed on cast/processed alloys that maintain a single-phase disordered BCC structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the disordered BCC solid solution, with reduced lattice distortion caused by a lower electronegativity difference between constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: Reducing the high Mo fraction diminishes the localized bonding rigidity associated with the large electronegativity difference. The additional Nb, known from prior studies to enhance ductility, compensates for the reduction in Mo’s solid solution strengthening, resulting in improved dislocation mobility and enhanced plasticity without a major drop in yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit increased room-temperature plastic strain (improved ductility) while retaining a compressive yield strength close to ~1719 MPa. Any loss of strength is anticipated to be minor if the substitution is optimized.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo with high strength but low plasticity under room-temperature compression.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow compositional window where Mo is partially reduced and Nb is correspondingly increased. Excessive reduction of Mo might compromise the solid solution strengthening, and the effect may be limited to alloys maintaining a disordered BCC structure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative shifts in yield strength and plastic strain improvements are uncertain and will depend on the amount of substitution; further experimental tuning is required to balance strength and ductility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys where a fixed percentage (e.g., 25% of the Mo content) is substituted with Nb, keeping the other elements (Nb, Zr, Ti, Hf) at their equiatomic ratios. Process the alloys under the same conditions to ensure the formation of a disordered BCC phase. Conduct room-temperature compression tests to record the compressive yield strength and the uniform plastic strain of each composition.
measurements: Uniform plastic strain (percentage elongation before failure)
Microstructural analysis (to confirm retention of disordered BCC structure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in room-temperature ductility (plastic strain), or if the compressive yield strength decreases by more than approximately 15% relative to the baseline equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. AbstractA series of TaNbVTiAlx (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with high specific strength and reasonable plasticity were prepared using powder metallurgy (P/M) technology. This paper studied their microstructure and compression properties. The results show that all the TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs exhibited a single BCC solid solution microstructure with no elemental segregation. The P/M TaNbVTiAlx RHEAs showed excellent room-temperature specific strength (207.11 MPa*cm3/g) and high-temperature specific strength (88.37 MPa*cm3/g at 900 °C and 16.03 MPa*cm3/g at 1200 °C), with reasonable plasticity, suggesting that these RHEAs have potential to be applied at temperatures >1200 °C. The reasons for the excellent mechanical properties of P/M TaNbVTiAl0.2 RHEA were the uniform microstructure and solid solution strengthening effect.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, refractory alloy, powder metallurgy, specific strength, ductile
